articles.title: Project ‘C430L’: How Russia secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles
articles.summary: International News: Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles under a multiyear covert programme codenamed “C430L,” in what expert.
articles.body: Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles under a multiyear covert programme codenamed “C430L,” in what experts say could be one of the most significant known transfers of strategic military technology from Moscow to Tehran, the Financial Times reported.According to the FT’s investigation, which is based on leaked Russian correspondence and an analysis of military patents, the programme began in 2023, well before the ongoing US-Iran war, but has continued into the current conflict in the Middle East.The report noted that the C430L programme is primarily aimed at helping Iran develop a ramjet propulsion system, an engine that enables a cruise missile to sustain speeds several times faster than the speed of sound. Missile and military experts say the technology was almost certainly intended for anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles."This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades. A programme like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia," Fabian Hinz, an expert on Iranian missiles, told FT.Tehran is reported to have built and flight-tested the ramjet propulsion system, although there is no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has been deployed so far.Why supersonic cruise missilesSupersonic cruise missiles combine high speed with the ability to fly at low altitudes, reducing the time available for sophisticated air and missile defence systems to detect and intercept them. This is particularly relevant for Iran in the Gulf, where the US and its regional allies operate advanced land- and sea-based defence systems.“For the Iranians, this would give them a qualitatively new strategic weapon system that could threaten US Navy vessels,” Jim Lamson, a former Iran-focused military analyst with the CIA, said.Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, arranged the programme and co-ordinated the project with NPO Mashinostroyenia, a Russian rocket design bureau.Washington sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia in 2014, describing it as a major Russian rocketry company involved in cruise missile systems launched from ships, submarines and ground platforms, as well as work supporting Moscow’s strategic nuclear forces, including intercontinental ballistic missiles.Leaked travel records show that Russian arms export officials and several senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers made repeated trips to Iran before the C430L contract was formally signed with Tehran’s Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics in November 2023.How project C430L unfoldedC430L involved some of NPO Mashinostroyenia’s most senior missile engineers, several of whom made repeated trips to Tehran in the lead-up to the formal signing of the contract.By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received a large cache of Iranian technical material on the ramjet propulsion system. Russian engineers analysed data from an Iranian flight test and sent Tehran a detailed list of questions about the system’s performance.They sought information on changes to the fuel system, combustion stability, air intake and engine nozzle. They also wanted to know whether the ramjet had continued operating after the telemetry provided by Iran — data showing the engine’s performance during flight — ended less than a minute into the test.In April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending a delegation of about two dozen Russian specialists to Iran for technical consultations under C430L. The same correspondence asked Tehran to respond to the engineers’ questions about the flight-test telemetry before the proposed visit, linking the mission directly to the technical assessment of Iran’s propulsion system.The leaked correspondence shows that the C430L programme continued into 2026, after the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Moscow preparing technical reports for Tehran and the two sides discussing the next phase of development.A June 2026 letter from Rosoboronexport showed that the parties were still negotiating elements of the next phase and planning further discussions on Russian technical reports. However, it remains unclear whether that phase of the programme has begun.

articles.title: Apple added these MacBooks to its ‘obsolete list’: What it means for users
articles.summary: Tech News News: Apple has officially added the 2018 Retina MacBook Air, the 13‑inch 2018 MacBook Pro (four Thunderbolt 3 ports), and the 13‑inch 2017 MacBook Pro (two.
articles.body: Apple has officially added the 2018 Retina MacBook Air, the 13‑inch 2018 MacBook Pro (four Thunderbolt 3 ports), and the 13‑inch 2017 MacBook Pro (two Thunderbolt 3 ports) to its obsolete products list. This means that the users of the above mentioned MacBook will not be able to receive hardware repairs. All three had previously been sitting on Apple's separate "vintage" list before being moved into the more restrictive obsolete category.How Apple's vintage and obsolete system worksApple's classification system runs on a fixed timeline. A product is added to the vintage list once five years have passed since Apple last distributed it for sale, and it graduates to obsolete status at the seven-year mark. The distinction between the two categories matters significantly for owners: vintage products can still be repaired at Apple retail stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers as long as Apple has the necessary parts on hand. Obsolete devices, by contrast, are generally no longer eligible for repair at all, and Apple stops manufacturing replacement components for them going forward.What it means for usersOwners of these devices should be aware of the following:* No official repairs for obsolete products like the iPad mini 4.* Limited service for vintage products like the 2017 MacBook Air, depending on parts availability.* Software updates are unlikely, which may affect app compatibility and security.* Third-party repair options may be the only alternative for maintenance.A look back at what made these models notableThe 2018 MacBook Air held a particular significance in the product line's history — it was the first Air model to include Touch ID and a Retina display, following earlier Air models that used a lower-resolution, less vibrant non-Retina screen. That same year also marked a broader redesign for the Air line, introducing smaller bezels and a thinner, lighter overall chassis.The 2017 MacBook Pro, meanwhile, ran on Intel's Kaby Lake processors and represented a fairly minor processor-focused update with few other significant changes. The following year's 2018 refresh added True Tone display support for the first time, along with a third-generation butterfly keyboard.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: ‘Pre-event indications’: Did Nepal miss warning signs before deadly floods? What report says
articles.summary: South Asia News: The glacier collapse that triggered a devastating landslide and flash floods along the Nepal-China border, killing over 1,100 showed visible signs of .
articles.body: The glacier collapse that triggered a devastating landslide and flash floods along the Nepal-China border, killing over 1,100 showed visible signs of instability days before the disaster, according to a new report by the HiRISK scientific consortium.Also Read | ‘Every rescue now a miracle’: 4,462 still missing in Nepal, hopes dimScientists said there were “pre-event indications”, including meltwater that had turned visibly brown and signs of a crack propagating into the surrounding bedrock slope.The findings have raised fresh questions over the lack of operational early warning systems for glacier-related hazards in the remote Himalayan region, with scientists saying more comprehensive systems downstream could have saved a “significant number of lives”. Warning signs before collapse?The HiRISK report, published last week, cited by CNN, examined the physical changes preceding the glacier collapse and the potential for early detection.“In hindsight, there were some pre-event indications,” the scientists said, pointing to visibly brown meltwater and a crack that was propagating into the surrounding bedrock slope days before the collapse.However, detecting such changes in a remote, high-altitude environment remains difficult. The report said early warning systems had recently been established in the region to monitor several glacial lakes in China, but no operational system was in place specifically for glacier-related hazards in the area where the collapse occurred.Also Read | Nepal tragedy: Owners missing, dog refuses to leave flood-hit Trishuli homeOnce the collapse began, the speed of the initial landslide meant conventional warning systems would likely have provided too little time to evacuate a border checkpoint that was among the first areas hit.Further downstream, however, there may have been more time to respond.The scientists said comprehensive early warning systems capable of providing 10 minutes or more of advance notice could have saved a “significant number of lives”.The finding stressed the need for systems that can monitor not only glacial lakes but also unstable glaciers and surrounding mountain slopes, while ensuring warnings reach vulnerable communities downstream. Death toll rises to 1,127As the cause and rescue ops continue, 1,127 people have died in the floods, according to Nepal Police. A total of 45 bodies have been recovered from Rasuwa, 155 from Nuwakot, 59 from Dhading, 348 from Chitwan, 66 from Gorkha, 38 from Tanahun, 217 from Nawalparasi East and 190 from Nawalparasi West.The death toll has risen to 1,127, with 45 bodies recovered in Rasuwa, 155 in Nuwakot, 59 in Dhading, 348 in Chitwan, 66 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 217 in Nawalparasi East and 190 in Nawalparasi West. Nine bodies have also been recovered in India. So far, only 95 of the total recovered bodies have been identified and handed over to their families.The disaster has also renewed calls for greater cooperation between Nepal and China in monitoring hazards across the Himalayas.Chinese and Nepali authorities had met as recently as May to discuss strengthening cooperation on monitoring natural hazards in the region, according to a government official who attended the meeting.Experts say better cross-border information sharing is particularly important because mountain hazards can rapidly affect communities and infrastructure on either side of the border.“There is almost no way that anyone could have detected this event prior – it happened in a blind spot … (making it) extremely difficult to detect,” Austin Lord, a senior fellow in the Energy, Water and Sustainability programme at the Stimson Center, wrote in a recent commentary.He also highlighted “how greater communication, information sharing, and collaborative analysis of transboundary risks between Nepal and China are sorely needed.”India also stepped up to assist Nepal’s rescue operations, deploying specialised Army teams to work alongside Nepali forces at the Chilime and Langtang tunnel sites. The teams have been navigating difficult terrain and unstable conditions as they search for missing people.Read more: India steps in with emergency helplines for stranded nationalsOther reports also highlighted disaster possibilityThe HiRISK report is separate from two major reports released by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) in March 2026.The ICIMOD reports examined longer-term changes across the Hindu Kush Himalaya and warned that accelerating glacier loss was increasing the risks of cryosphere-related hazards, including glacial lake outburst floods.They found that HKH glaciers lost around 12 per cent of their total area and 9 per cent of their estimated ice reserves between 1990 and 2020, while glacier ice loss had doubled after 2000.The reports also found that the region’s smallest glaciers were shrinking particularly rapidly, with three-fourths of HKH glaciers falling into the vulnerable category of less than 0.5 square kilometres.ICIMOD also highlighted major gaps in glacier monitoring. Its 2026 Glacier Outlook found that only seven of 38 monitored glaciers met the global benchmark monitoring standards set by the World Glacier Monitoring Service, while several major glacierised regions remained largely unmonitored.“This isn’t a distant problem; it’s a crisis unfolding in real-time, with new disasters every summer and monsoon,” ICIMOD Director General Pema Gyamtsho said.Thus, the ICIMOD reports provided a broad assessment of the region’s accelerating glacier loss and the risks it creates, while the new HiRISK report focuses specifically on the recent disaster, including the physical warning signs before the collapse and whether early warning systems could have reduced casualties.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: California lawmakers are moving $125 million toward buying a 162-acre former Bay Area racetrack; the $175 million deal would turn it into a major public waterfront park
articles.summary: US News: California lawmakers are moving forward with $125 million in state funding to help purchase the former Golden Gate Fields racetrack and transform the .
articles.body: California lawmakers are moving forward with $125 million in state funding to help purchase the former Golden Gate Fields racetrack and transform the roughly 162-acre Bay Area property into a major public waterfront park, according to reporting by Albany Scanner and San Francisco Chronicle, as well as information from the East Bay Regional Park District (EBRPD). The funding, proposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, is part of the state budget and would come from Proposition 4, the climate bond approved by California voters in 2024. The money still requires legislative approval and must be signed by Newsom before it is secured. The proposed state contribution would be a major step toward closing the gap on a $175 million purchase that could permanently change the East Bay shoreline.From racetrack to waterfront parkGolden Gate Fields, which straddles Albany and Berkeley, operated as a horse-racing facility until it closed in June 2024. The property covers approximately 162 acres, with the majority in Albany and roughly 40 acres in Berkeley.In February 2026, the Trust for Public Land (TPL) secured an option agreement giving it the exclusive right to purchase the property with the goal of creating a public park and shoreline open space. If the purchase goes through, ownership would be transferred to the East Bay Regional Park District, which would become the site’s long-term steward. The proposed park could eventually include habitat restoration, recreational facilities, improved shoreline access and connections to nearby trails and parks.The $125 million still isn’t enoughThe purchase price is $175 million. The Park District had previously committed $20 million from voter-approved Measure WW funds toward acquiring the property. If the full $125 million state allocation is approved, that would leave roughly $30 million still to be raised.TPL and EBRPD are working to assemble the remaining funding from public and philanthropic sources. The deadline matters: TPL must secure the financing by early 2027, with the transaction expected to close in spring 2027 if the funding package comes together.And buying the land won’t be the end of the expense. The purchase price includes removal of existing above-ground structures, but officials have not yet released a full estimate for preparing and developing the property as a public park.What would happen after the purchase?Residents should not expect to walk into a finished park immediately after the sale. According to EBRPD, 2027 to 2029 would be devoted largely to a public planning process, involving Albany, Berkeley, residents and other stakeholders.Community input would help determine priorities for habitat restoration, recreation, access points and connections to surrounding neighbourhoods and regional trails. Actual park construction would happen in phases after 2029, depending on available funding.The Bay Trail is expected to remain open, while broader public access to the property would expand gradually as safety improvements, restoration and infrastructure work are completed.What about housing?For now, the proposal is explicitly centred on a public park. TPL and EBRPD say the property is not currently zoned for housing in Albany or Berkeley. The future park could include habitat restoration, recreation and other compatible uses, with the precise vision to emerge through the public planning process.The project is also being framed as a way to create a more connected stretch of East Bay waterfront, linking Golden Gate Fields with nearby open spaces including the Albany Bulb, McLaughlin Eastshore State Park and other shoreline parks.A financial question for AlbanyThe transformation could bring a major benefit to the region, but it also presents a financial challenge for Albany. Before the racetrack closed, Golden Gate Fields was among the city’s significant commercial taxpayers. According to Albany’s analysis, the property generated about $1.1 million annually in special revenues for the city and approximately $700,000 for Albany Unified School District.The city estimates that another $150,000 to $300,000 a year went toward its general fund through racetrack, sales, business-license and utility-users’ taxes. If the property becomes tax-exempt under nonprofit ownership, much of that revenue could disappear, potentially putting pressure on city services.A long-awaited transformationFor EBRPD officials, however, the opportunity extends beyond converting a former racetrack. The proposed park could expand public access to San Francisco Bay, restore habitat and strengthen connections between existing waterfront parks and trails.“This is an extraordinary opportunity to create a more connected system of parks and trails,” EBRPD General Manager Max Korten said. But before the vision becomes reality, there is still a $30 million funding gap, legislative approval and years of planning ahead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1930, Americans carried fish into Olympic's fishless mountain lakes; 1.6 million trout later scientists are finding the ecological cost
articles.summary: US News: Beginning in 1930, more than 1.6 million fish were carried by horseback or dropped from aircraft into the naturally fishless mountain lakes of what is.
articles.body: Beginning in 1930, more than 1.6 million fish were carried by horseback or dropped from aircraft into the naturally fishless mountain lakes of what is now Olympic National Park, creating recreational fishing opportunities in waters that had never supported fish populations before. Most lakes were stocked only once, although some were restocked repeatedly, with individual lakes receiving as many as 18 stocking events over the following decades. The introductions fundamentally changed ecosystems that had developed without fish predators, particularly for native amphibians that had evolved in these isolated mountain waters. Nearly a century later, researchers have completed the first comprehensive survey of fish and amphibian distributions across 117 remote lakes in and around Olympic National Park. Using environmental DNA, or eDNA, collected between 2019 and 2021, the team has now mapped where introduced fish remain and found that their presence is associated with lower detection rates for some native amphibians, while other species continue to coexist with fish by using habitats beyond their reach.How researchers used eDNA to survey 117 remote mountain lakesResearchers surveyed 117 lakes between 2019 and 2021, covering roughly 500 miles of travel and more than 200,000 feet of cumulative elevation gain while collecting water samples for environmental DNA. The technique detects genetic material organisms leave behind in their surroundings, allowing researchers to determine whether particular fish and amphibian species were present without having to capture every animal in each remote lake. The survey detected introduced fish in 59 of the 117 lakes examined. Amphibians were detected without fish in 52 lakes, while fish and amphibians were detected together in 45 lakes and fish were detected without amphibians in 14 lakes. Six lakes produced no detections of either group. The survey also identified fish in 21 lakes where researchers could find no historical record of stocking. The study notes several possible explanations, including incomplete historical records, unauthorised fish introductions or false-positive detections, while the National Park Service says the findings suggest some fish may have been introduced independently of the official stocking program. The results provide a much more complete picture of the distribution of introduced fish than historical stocking records alone could provide.Why some amphibians declined near fish while others continued to coexistThe survey found that long-toed salamanders and rough-skinned newts were less likely to be detected in lakes where introduced fish were present, consistent with previous research showing that nonnative trout can affect native amphibians. But the researchers did not find that every amphibian species disappeared wherever fish occurred. In fact, fish and amphibians were detected together in 45 lakes, about 3.2 times as many lakes as those where fish were detected without amphibians. Jeff Duda, an ecologist with the U.S. Geological Survey and a co-author of the study, said researchers had expected amphibians to struggle in lakes containing fish but found that some species appear capable of coexisting with them. One important advantage amphibians have is that they are not confined to the water. Species can use terrestrial areas around lakes or move into small, temporary wetlands and ponds where fish cannot establish themselves. Cascades frogs provide an example: researchers note that they may breed in ephemeral wetlands and ponds adjacent to lakes, allowing their eggs and tadpoles to develop in habitats without fish. That flexibility may help explain why some amphibians remain widespread even after decades of fish introductions, while species that depend more heavily on permanent lakes appear more vulnerable.Why climate change could make the fish problem harder for Olympic's amphibiansThe remaining question is what happens as the mountain environment itself changes. The small seasonal wetlands that provide amphibians with refuges from fish are particularly vulnerable to warming temperatures and declining snowpack because they depend on water remaining on the landscape long enough for breeding to occur. The National Park Service notes that the Olympic Range's snowpack was only 26% of its 30-year normal in the year of its accompanying report, illustrating the increasingly difficult conditions facing these temporary habitats. That creates a potential double pressure: amphibians already face predation and competition from introduced fish in permanent lakes, while the alternative wetlands that allow some species to avoid fish may become less reliable as the climate warms. Other national parks have provided evidence that removing introduced fish can benefit native amphibians. The National Park Service points to work at Mount Rainier and North Cascades national parks showing increases in native amphibian populations where fish are absent. For Olympic, however, the new eDNA survey provides something that has been missing for decades: a park-wide picture of where introduced fish and native amphibians are found today. That baseline gives researchers and park managers a way to track future changes and determine where fish removal or other conservation measures could have the greatest benefit as both introduced predators and climate change continue reshaping the park's high-elevation lakes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the day by Apple’s CEO John Ternus: “Build what interests you, build what excites you, but above all…”
articles.summary: Tech News News: John Ternus has spent much of his career working behind products that people use every day, dealing with the engineering decisions that determine how .
articles.body: John Ternus has spent much of his career working behind products that people use every day, dealing with the engineering decisions that determine how those products look, work and hold up over time. Now, as Apple’s chief executive, his words about building have a wider audience. In a 2024 commencement address at the University of Pennsylvania, Ternus told graduates to build things that interest and excite them, while making sure those things fit their values. The advice is straightforward, but the final part changes its meaning. It is not simply about finding enjoyable work or chasing an interesting idea. It asks people to think about what they are creating and whether it reflects the principles they want to stand behind. Coming from an engineer whose career has centred on designing and developing hardware, the choice of the word 'build' is particularly fitting.Quote of the day by John Ternus“Build what interests you, build what excites you, but above all else, build it in a way that aligns with your values.”What John Ternus meant by building around your valuesThe quote was delivered by Ternus during his 2024 commencement speech at the University of Pennsylvania, where he had studied mechanical engineering. The first part of Ternus’s advice is about curiosity. People tend to spend a great deal of their working lives on a relatively small number of subjects, so having a genuine interest in the problem can make a difference.Excitement adds something slightly different. Being interested in a subject does not necessarily mean finding every part of the work enjoyable. Difficult projects can involve repetition, setbacks and long stretches when progress is hard to see. Ternus’s point is not that work should always be fun. It is that there should be something about the work that keeps a person engaged with it.Then comes the qualification: values come first. That shifts the quote away from simple career advice. A project can be technically impressive or personally exciting and still not be something a person wants to help create. Values provide the boundary around the other two ideas.Ternus built his career on the engineering side of AppleTernus’s own professional background makes the language of building especially appropriate.He studied mechanical engineering at the University of Pennsylvania before beginning his career at Virtual Research Systems. He joined Apple in 2001, initially working within the company’s product design organisation. Over the years, his responsibilities expanded across hardware engineering and some of Apple’s most recognisable products.Apple says Ternus became vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and joined the company’s executive team in 2021. His rise was therefore closely tied to the technical side of the company rather than following a conventional route through finance or sales.Ternus's work went far beyond how an Apple device lookedTernus eventually became senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, overseeing the teams responsible for Apple’s hardware development.That role placed him close to the practical process of turning ideas into finished products. Hardware engineering involves far more than the appearance of a device. Materials, reliability, manufacturing, durability and the interaction between different components all have to work together.The position also meant working across several product categories at once. A decision that makes sense for one device may not necessarily work for another. Engineering teams have to balance performance, size, cost, manufacturing constraints and the experience of the person using the finished product.Ternus became Apple CEO in 2026Apple announced in April 2026 that Cook would become executive chairman and Ternus would become CEO on September 1, 2026. His appointment followed years of increasing responsibility within the company.He therefore took over after more than two decades at Apple, much of that time spent working on hardware.The transition also meant that an engineer with extensive experience in product development moved into the role responsible for the company as a whole.Ternus's three-part test adds a missing question to career adviceTernus’s quote can be read as a simple three-question test.First, does the subject genuinely interest you?Second, is there something about the work that excites you enough to keep learning and improving?Third, does what you are building fit with your values?The third question is the one that prevents the advice from becoming another version of “follow your passion”.Interest can tell someone where to look. Excitement can help sustain attention. Values can help determine where the line should be drawn.Building does not mean getting everything rightThere is also an important implication in the word “build”.A finished product is usually the visible result of many versions that never reached the public. Ideas are tested, changed, rejected and rebuilt. The same can happen with a career.Ternus’s own path at Apple was not a single leap from engineer to chief executive. He moved through different positions and took on broader responsibilities over many years.That makes the quote less about finding one perfect project and more about deciding what is worth continuing to work on. Sometimes the first version is wrong. That does not necessarily mean the entire idea has failed. It may simply need to be rebuilt.Lessons to learn from John Ternus’s quoteLet curiosity guide your directionChoose something that keeps you engagedDo not follow passion blindlyKeep your values involved in your decisionsThink beyond the finished resultKnow what is worth your effortBalance ambition with principlesBuild something you can stand behindGet the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Sister's regular social media spirals discovered after her death
articles.summary: The sister of Blake Gallier, from Kent, says she "needed to know" what she watched before her death.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains details and references to suicide

Blake Gallier's death in October came as a surprise to her family, from Gravesend in Kent.

Her sister Tayla Gallier, 19, told the BBC she looked through Blake's phone after her death, having felt she "needed to know" what content her sibling had seen prior to her death.

Gallier found her sister had watched "videos talking about self-harming, suicidal ideation" and had been going through a spiral "night after night".

According to the older sibling, the content Blake Gallier had been viewing "was progressively getting more serious and severe".

The 19-year-old said it "wasn't social media that killed my sister" but she thought it was "the tipping point".

"No one gets the idea of doing that to themselves from school, from their family, from their friends," she said.

"The only place you can get that idea is from social media and I think that's the biggest problem."

Tayla Gallier said she did not think all social media was negative but that it was "awful that that sort of stuff can be allowed on there".

"Clearly there are not enough regulations and they're not enforced enough," she told the BBC.

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport has been contacted for comment.

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line .

Tayla Gallier described her sister as "full of energy all the time".

"She was one of the most annoying people ever," she said. "I think when you have younger siblings they do everything to get on your nerves."

The girls' mother Gemma Best said the younger sister was a "very normal teenager" who was the "life and soul at every party" and "absolutely loved her friends".

Best said: "It's just awful as a parent, but I wasn't aware of all of the apps that she had on her phone."

She says she sometimes still finds it "hard to believe" that her daughter is not here because "there were no signs in any shape or form".

Blake Gallier's family are setting up a charity - Blake's Pink Promise - in order to "keep Blake's memory alive", in part by funding counselling in schools.

"We've currently counselled 77 children and two adults across four different schools and we're looking to go into two further schools in October," Best said.

"We want to support our local community because they're the ones that are helping us to fundraise."

articles.title: "My house was destroyed by a neighbour's garden bonfire"
articles.summary: Houses on the terrace in Sheffield have been targeted by burglars since the fire in July.
articles.body:
For Robert Marsden, seeing his home go up in flames and almost completely destroyed was "soul-destroying".

Marsden's house was part of a terrace in Sheffield which suffered major damage after a neighbour's garden bonfire spread out of control during the July heatwaves.

Marsden lost around 70% of his family home and even slept inside the charred shell for two weeks after burglars targeted one of the other damaged houses.

He said: "It was just soul-destroying to see everything that you've got for your family, gone - and it was gone in minutes."

Five properties on Fox Hill Road in Grenoside were affected by the fire which spread from back gardens at about 04:00 BST on 23 July.

A 59-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage – arson endangering life, and criminal damage – arson not endangering life. He has since been released on bail pending further investigations.

Several residents had to be evacuated and were offered emergency accommodation, with two men suffering minor injuries, according to South Yorkshire Police.

Marsden was away visiting relatives at the time, and the only person in the house was his daughter-in-law.

She lives in the property with Marsden's son, his 10-year-old daughter and his granddaughter, 12.

He said: "That was the main thing. My daughter was meant to stay there with her that night.

"And, but for the grace of God, she decided at 10 o'clock that night to stay with her mum instead, or she would have been in the bedroom where all that damage occurred."

Marsden was called in the early hours of the morning about the fire, and rushed back to find "every ceiling was down".

"There was 60 years worth of soot mixed in with thousands of gallons of water and no roof."

A builder by trade, Marsden has decided to rebuild his home himself, with the "tremendous help" of friends who also work in the industry.

He is currently renting a property, but initially stayed at the roofless house for two weeks to prevent it from being looted.

Marsden said his neighbour had already been targeted and had their jewellery stolen.

"So that's why I moved back into my own house to stop what we had got left from being taken.

"I was so frightened - not that I've not got a million pounds worth of stuff hiding around - it's just the bits that we had left."

He added: "I refused to let that go as well."

Marsden said during that fortnight he was not "probably not functioning at 100% mentally" and it was damp with a constant smell of burning. His electricity had been cut off, but has since been reconnected.

"I wouldn't advise it - but it was a protection mode for what we've got," he added.

Marsden was assisted by councillor Yvonne Sykes, who represents the Southey ward on Sheffield City Council and pushed for him to be found suitable accommodation.

"These are far from ideal living conditions and one of the worst and most shocking things about this is that some of the properties were burgled in the aftermath of the fire."

Marsden is waiting for his insurance company to assess the damage and in the meantime is doing repairs himself.

Sykes added: "This has been a pretty traumatic event, not just for Rob but for this whole community."

articles.title: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel is expanding positions
articles.summary: A BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force, which says Israeli troops are fortifying positions and continuing demolitions.
articles.body:
The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.

Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.

This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.

Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.

Led by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.

The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.

We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.

In a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.

According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict.

"In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."

Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.

In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.

In June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.

As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory.

"[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."

Israeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.

Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.

The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October.

"The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."

articles.title: Woking school opens uniform shop to sell items 'at cost'
articles.summary: The Winston Churchill School in Woking says the approach cuts £20 off the price of blazers.
articles.body:
A secondary school in Surrey has secured its own uniform supplier so it can sell items at cost to pupils.

The Winston Churchill School in Woking opened its own uniform shop to cut back to costs for families, where parents can order items on site or online, with clothing including skirts, ties and PE kit available at no markup from what it cost the school.

Head teacher Zoe Johnson-Walker said that the approach had cut £20 off the cost of school blazers compared to the previous school year.

"We've been trying to reduce the cost of our uniform over a couple of years," she told the BBC.

The school redesigned its uniform for 2026-27, coinciding with new government rules limiting secondary schools to three branded items , plus a branded tie.

According to the Department for Education, the new rules would save parents up to £50.

"Parents have told us they want fewer costly branded items – and that's exactly what we're delivering," a spokesperson said.

"School uniform matters, but it shouldn't break the bank."

Johnson-Walker said That the school had proposed removing its branded blazers from its uniform as it was "one of our most expensive items" but had found "quite a large demand from parents to sell it with the badge on".

"We've managed to do a negotiation with our supplier which means that there's no additional cost to parents to have a badged item," she said.

She added that the school had scrapped branded PE tops but was selling plain, black PE shirts in its uniform shop after requests from parents.

"We're also trying to maintain standards because uniform, as far as we're concerned, is quite levelling," Johnson-Walker added.

Nicola Dawes, chief executive at family support charity Stripey Stork, said that the back-to-school period put "additional pressure on families from a cost perspective".

The organisation gave out more than 15,000 uniform items and about 1,500 pairs of school shoes over the summer under its School Days campaign.

The scheme, in its fourth year, received council funding and donations of pre-loved items from the community.

"It's something we've put a bigger priority on it in terms of our work because we realise how important it is," Dawes said.

articles.title: More sea protection causing 'sleepless nights' for Jersey fishers
articles.body:
A Jersey fisherman has said the expansion of marine protected areas is threatening the industry's future, but the approval of five additional bluefin tuna licences had offered a much-needed boost.

New rules mean the area of sea protected from trawling and dredging has more than tripled . Conservationists said the changes would protect important areas of sea and improve the long-term health of fish stocks.

Dishers have welcomed the extra tuna licences , but said the fishery was only seasonal and would not make up for the fishing areas lost.

Environment Minister Mary Le Hegarat said Jersey's seas were "one of the island's greatest natural assets" and needed continuous protection.

"These measures are evidence-led, have been developed through extensive consultation and form an important part of our long-term vision for the management of Jersey's marine environment," she said.

The head of the Jersey Fishermen's Association, Stephen Viney, said the expansion of the marine protected areas had been a "slow car crash coming" for many in the industry and protections had gone too far.

"We're losing some of the most productive grounds that we fish. We are in a situation now where the fishing industry is struggling. It probably couldn't have come at a worse time, to be honest.

"We've known it's been coming, but it would have been nice to have something else to fill the gap.

"These areas have been fished for hundreds of years and they're still producing good catches and they have been traditionally very important to the industry."

Despite concerns over protected areas, Viney said the opportunity to fish for bluefin tuna has "brought a bit of hope".

Kirstie Thorpe-Jones, of the Bass & Lobster seafood restaurant said people had been "so excited" to see tuna on the menu.

"It's a great advantage for us. We offer a lot of local things, so anything that comes to us that's local we're always keen to put it on the menu", she said.

Kevin McIlwee, founder of Jersey Marine Conservation, said putting in the protections was evidence-based, and they were designed to prevent damage to a range of habitats, including maerl (calcified seaweed) beds.

McIlwee acknowledged fishers were being "squeezed into smaller areas", but it was down to the government to look at the "management of how many vessels there are, how often they're fishing and what particular species they're targeting".

Freddie Watson, from the Blue Marine Foundation conservation charity, said the protected areas had been chosen because they contained "very sensitive and important habitats" for maerl, seagrass, and kelp

He said: "They're very sensitive so we have to do everything we can to protect them for the long run.

Watson said maerl in particular was especially important: "it hosts probably the highest amount of biodiversity in our waters".

He said: "At one point, about 200 species have been recorded in a small area, so it's great for generating biodiversity and improving recruitment of certain species such as scallops and lobsters.

"It also plays that role in storing and locking down carbon."

"If we manage our marine environment better, then we'll have species coming back in healthier populations", he added.

articles.title: Brighton theatre's concern over Bhasvic football pitches plan
articles.summary: Brighton Open Air Theatre says football pitches planned nearby would disrupt performances.
articles.body:
The manager of an open air theatre says he is disappointed that plans for artificial football pitches nearby have been recommended for approval, but wants to work to ensure the two sites can co-exist.

Brighton Open Air Theatre (Boat) says performances would be "essentially unviable" due to noise issues arising from proposed plans for pitches put forward by Brighton, Hove & Sussex Sixth Form College (Bhasvic).

Will Mytum, Boat's general manager, said that the plans would still affect unamplified performances despite mitigations put in place.

Plans for the pitches and multi-use game area go before Brighton & Hove City Council's planning committee on Wednesday.

Mytum said: "We think it will be incredibly disruptive to our operation and really put our theatre in jeopardy.

"We don't think the conditions would be acceptable to us. It would still clash with a lot of our performances.

"They are our neighbours, so if the plans are approved then we will have to work with them on it."

A report to the planning committee where the pitches were recommended for approval said they "would have the potential to result in significant disruption to Boat performances".

It added that "substantially reduced hours" put forward by Bhasvic could help to mitigate this, and early closures could be arranged "case by case between the applicant and Boat".

The report also said Boat had 125 performances scheduled, this year and the amended hours would mean the pitches would be in use at the same time on only seven occasions, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Mytum said the theatre had put forward an alternative suggestion for time restrictions, which he hoped the planning committee would accept.

Brighton & Hove Planning Committee will meet at 14:00 BST on Wednesday, at Hove Town Hall.

articles.title: Clarks Shoemakers Museum shares people's sentimental footwear memories
articles.summary: The Shoemakers Museum is marking its first anniversary by exhibiting shoes from local people.
articles.body:
Peoples' sentimental footwear, including wedding shoes and a special retirement present, is being celebrated in a new exhibition.

Somerset's Clarks Shoemakers Museum in Street is marking its first anniversary by exhibiting footwear from local people that hold a unique memory.

They have chosen 12 shoes from the community, marking the 12 months that the museum has been open.

Liz Fox, who helped organise the exhibition, said: "They're all shoes that evoke memories and have a close sentimental connection with times that have passed."

Fox contributed her white Dr Martens wedding boots that are embossed with a nature theme.

"We got married on a farm out near Petherton. We arrived by tractor. I had a very traditional wedding dress but with these boots tucked under," Fox said.

"Unfortunately it didn't last; we were married 10 years - but the shoes did last."

The museum opened in September 2025 and showcases 200 years of Clarks' shoemaking history.

The exhibition, which is running until 6 September, also includes the brand's famous Desert Boot that was presented to Pat Snee with his face on when he retired from Clarks after 50 years.

"They are significant because they were being built long before I was even born," Snee said.

Snee started working for Clarks in 1969 in Radstock, when he was 15 years old and fresh out of school.

"I worked my way up right into the company. I came off the shop floor into management in the 80s," Snee said.

Snee said his main memory of his time with Clarks was when he was asked to turn the Christmas lights on.

"That year, the CEO said he wanted me to turn the lights on because I was the longest-serving employee," Snee said.

"For many years I worked with Clarks, I've always been asked to turn the lights off as I go out and this is the first time I've ever been asked to turn the lights on."

Rosie Martin, director at the Shoemakers Museum, contributed two of her family's shoes to the exhibition.

One of them is a black Italian men's shoe, belonging to her husband.

"He got it at the exact moment [when] the Italian Lira changed to the Euro and he thought he found a very cheap Italian shoe in Lira but it turned out it was actually very expensive," Martin said.

Martin and her husband married in 2004 and he wore the shoes to the wedding.

"He decided to pass them on to our son who is 19 now and going off to university," Martin added.

articles.title: Oxfordshire charity concerned more horses being given up over costs
articles.summary: An Oxfordshire animal welfare charity says its Burford site is taking in 20 to 30 horses a month.
articles.body:
The rising cost of caring for horses is putting more owners under financial pressure, with an animal welfare charity reporting an increase in horses being given up.

The Blue Cross in Burford, Oxfordshire, says the situation has been made more difficult this year by the dry weather, leading to hay shortages and more expensive food prices.

The site is currently taking in 20 to 30 horses a month, and the charity across the UK saying it has seen a "160% surge in relinquished horses in recent years".

Admissions coordinator Freya Long says: "There's no grass, very little hay. I've started getting an increase in requests and I can only imagine it'll get higher with the cost of living."

The charity says the costs for owners can extend well beyond feed, with veterinary care, vaccinations, worming and farrier visits all essential to a horse's welfare.

Horse centre manger Vicki Alford adds: "It all adds up. We are finding, unfortunately, that people are contacting us because they can't financially look after their horses anymore."

In 2025, The RSPCA found that the nature of the equine crisis had shifted from abandonment to more general welfare issues.

Its research identified a combination of factors, including a lack of:

Practical knowledge, skills and experience in caring for equines

Suitable facilities and space for turn-out, grazing and socialisation

Provision and planning for lifetime welfare and care of horses

The charity said these issues have been enhanced by increases in the cost of living over recent years.

The Blue Cross said it wants owners to ask for help before financial difficulties begin to affect the welfare of their animals.

Alford says: "We absolutely encourage this, we want people to come to us..........before their horses get too far down the line.

"Please come to us. We are here to help and we will not judge."

articles.title: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity; decades later scientists found the plantations were changing groundwater but not the soil nature
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater proce.
articles.body: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater processes behind the problem. A long-running experiment in south-western Australia later showed that the effects of such plantations were more complicated than simply planting trees and waiting for the land to recover. Researchers established a mixed eucalyptus plantation above a saline seep in 1976 and monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped. Published in ‘Agricultural Water Management,’ the research offers a revealing look at why tree planting can influence groundwater and salinity without necessarily solving the underlying problem everywhere it is tried.How did eucalyptus plantations change groundwater and soil salinity in AustraliaThe study examined a plantation established on about 12% of a small farm catchment. The trees were planted above a saline seep, an area where salty groundwater had reached or approached the surface and damaged the land. The researchers wanted to identify eucalyptus species that could use large amounts of water and potentially help reclaim such affected areas. According to the study, the catchment contained two important groundwater systems. One was a deep aquifer in the lower part of the landscape and the other, a shallower seasonal aquifer. The researchers monitored changes in groundwater level and salinity using piezometers, allowing them to follow how conditions changed as the plantation developed.The results showed that the plantation was having a noticeable effect on water use. Changes in groundwater levels, along with observations of perched water, indicated that the trees were using more water than the nearby crop and pasture vegetation. This was an important finding because the basic idea behind planting trees in salt-affected agricultural landscapes was that trees could alter the movement of water through the soil. If less water moved downwards into the groundwater system, or if trees removed more water from the landscape, they could potentially help limit the processes that bring salt towards the surface.The groundwater changed, but the saline seep remainedThe researchers found that the plantation influenced groundwater chemistry as well as water levels. Chloride concentrations in the deep aquifer fell by approximately 20% between 1977 and 1984. The decline was greater at the middle of the slope than further downslope. This suggested that conditions beneath the catchment were changing, although the changes were not uniform across the landscape. At the same time, the study found larger stores of salt in the soil downslope than at the middle of the slope. There was also visual evidence that salt continued to be discharged extensively through the saline seep throughout the experiment. In other words, the trees were clearly affecting the local water system, but their presence did not bring the expected recovery of the seep. The research showed why this distinction matters. A plantation may increase water use and change groundwater conditions without having enough influence over the particular underground system responsible for a saline area.Why didn't the eucalyptus trees solve the salinity problemOne of the most important findings of the study concerned the location of the plantation. The researchers identified the site's underground geology as a significant reason why the trees failed to control the seepage. The plantation was located in an area where the relevant aquifer appeared to be ‘confined.’ That meant the groundwater system beneath the site was not easy for the trees to influence in the way researchers had hoped. This finding highlighted a practical limitation of tree-based approaches to salinity. Planting species that use substantial amounts of water may not be enough on its own. The location of groundwater, the way water moves through underground layers and the position of the plantation within the wider landscape can all affect the outcome. The study therefore showed that managing salinity is not simply a question of selecting the thirstiest trees. Understanding the underground environment is equally important.Some eucalyptus species performed better over 15 yearsThe experiment also compared the performance of different eucalyptus species. The original aim was to rank species partly according to water use, which the researchers assessed through factors including leaf area and survival. Tree growth was rapid during the early years of the experiment, continuing strongly until 1981. After that, growth declined. 15 years later, four species emerged as the most promising among those tested. These included ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx var. nana,’ ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx,’ ‘Eucalyptus occidentalis’ and ‘Eucalyptus sargentii.’ Their performance did not mean that the plantation had solved the saline seep problem. Instead, it showed that some species were better suited than others to the demanding conditions of the site. A tree can survive well and use considerable amounts of water while still being unable to alter a groundwater system enough to stop salt from reaching the surface.A long-term lesson from Australia's eucalyptus plantationsThe 15-year experiment provided a more realistic picture of what tree planting could not achieve in salt-affected farmland. The eucalyptus plantation used more water than the surrounding vegetation, and conditions in the deep groundwater system also shifted, including a significant fall in chloride concentration. Yet the saline seep continued to discharge salt. As per the study, this outcome was due to the underground conditions beneath the plantation. The research pointed towards a broader lesson that the success of planting trees depends not only on the trees, but also on the landscape in which they are planted. For areas struggling with rising groundwater and soil salinity, the findings suggest that planting eucalyptus can be a useful tool, but it is not a solution. Trees can change groundwater behaviour, without necessarily controlling the source of the problem. Only by monitoring the plantation for many years were researchers able to see both the benefits of greater tree water use and the limits imposed by the site's hidden groundwater system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: JioHotstar launches in UK, Canada and Singapore with new shows and live features
articles.summary: Tech News News: JioHotstar has launched in the UK, Canada and Singapore, bringing its Indian entertainment catalogue to audiences outside India. In a press release, t.
articles.body: JioHotstar has launched in the UK, Canada and Singapore, bringing its Indian entertainment catalogue to audiences outside India. In a press release, the company said that the “launch goes beyond taking JioHotstar’s extensive entertainment catalogue to new markets” and “brings audiences a new way to discover, watch and engage with entertainment combining 160K+ hours of content across 12+ languages and multiple genres with personalized recommendations, interactive features, flexible subscription options and a delightful product experience”.JioHotstar brings 160,000+ hours of Indian entertainment to international audienceJioHotstar offers content across several categories, including television, films, regional programming, non-fiction, kids' content and anime. The platform's library includes popular shows and originals such as Criminal Justice, Special Ops, Asur, Aarya, Pritam & Pedro, Heartbeat, Kerala Crime Files and Resort.Its film catalogue includes titles such as Dhurandhar, 12th Fail, Chhichhore, Kesari Chapter 2: The Untold Story of Jallianwala Bagh, Kill, Jab We Met and Vaazha. JioHotstar said it plans to add more than 30,000 hours of fresh content every year, giving users access to a continually expanding catalogue. The platform has kicked off its international launch with a diverse line-up of entertainment that includes:New Originals & Blockbuster Premieres: A slate of originals including Ali Baba Aur Chaalis Bhoot, Prince of Mollywood, Part Timers, The Court and more alongside blockbuster movie premieres through the year.Bigg Boss, Now Interactive: The iconic reality franchise Bigg Boss returns across six languages, and for the first time, audiences across Singapore, Canada and the UK will be able to vote LIVE across every edition, giving them the power to actively participate in and influence the game in real time. While audiences in Canada and the UK will have access to the 24x7 LIVE Feed, Canada will also be able to watch Bigg Boss Hindi 7 days ahead of its TV broadcast.A New Game Show Format: Audiences in Canada and Singapore can witness the magic of Anil Kapoor hosting India Ka Top 1 Percent, a new format that tests contestants’ logic and reasoning.Content from JioStar TV Channels with Early Access: Audiences can access content from JioStar television channels, including Star Plus, Colors, Star Vijay, Asianet, Star Jalsha and Star Pravah, with Before-TV access to popular shows in Singapore and Canada, including Anupama, Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai, Seher Hone Ko Hai, Azhagae Azhagu, while audiences in the UK can watch popular shows simultaneously with their TV broadcast, alongside regional and daily entertainment.JioHotstar subscription plans for UK, Canada and SingaporeJioHotstar is also introducing new quarterly subscription plans across all three markets for the first time. The updated pricing effective 2 nd September across markets is as follows:Commenting on JioHotstar’s international expansion and vision for global streaming, Amit Malhotra, Head – International Business, JioStar, said: “Streaming has spent the last decade competing on the size of its catalogue. We believe the bigger opportunity now is to reimagine how audiences experience entertainment; not just what they watch, but how they discover, engage with and shape the experience in real time. South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations and households. At the same time, audiences globally are increasingly seeking stories and cultures beyond their own. We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience - not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets.”He further added, “As we expand internationally, our ambition is to show what becomes possible when scale, language, cultural diversity, personalisation and deeper audience participation are built into the streaming experience from day one.”Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: “Civic sense died here…”; Gujarati tourists sing and clap loudly on a bus in Germany, leaving fellow passengers visibly uncomfortable
articles.summary: A video of a group of Gujarati tourists singing loudly inside a public bus in Germany has once again triggered the same old debate. “Civic sense”. How.
articles.body: A video of a group of Gujarati tourists singing loudly inside a public bus in Germany has once again triggered the same old debate. “Civic sense”. How disturbing others with shouting loudly can be celebrating your culture abroad? The clip shows the group singing together while other other passengers in the bus look quite shocked and quiet. Some look visibly uncomfortable and disgusted. The exact German city, bus route and date of the incident have not been independently established. But the video has gone viral for all the wrong reasons and has again put Indians in the wrong light.The controversy is not about Gujarati music or Indian celebrations but more about the place and how they are being expressed.Why the German bus video has attracted criticismFor many travellers, a public bus is only a way to reach one place to another. In Germany, as in much of Europe, passengers generally expect shared public transport to remain relatively silent. People may talk to companions, listen to music through headphones or use their phones, but loud group singing can easily become irritating.There is nothing inherently wrong with a group of tourists being happy. But the problem here arises when a shared space becomes an unwilling audience for that celebration.It also comes at a time when social media has made tourist behaviour itself part of the travel spectacle.Not the first timeThis is not the first time Indian tourists have faced backlash.In May 2026, a video from Vietnam showed Indian tourists performing Garba near a VietJet aircraft at an airport. The video generated backlash from all over. People questioned whether an airport operational area was an appropriate place for a spontaneous dance performance.Another clip from Hanoi's famous Train Street showed Indian tourists dancing to Chaiyya Chaiyya. The location itself is unusual: a narrow railway corridor where trains pass through a densely built-up neighbourhood. The video again raised questions about civic sense.Then back in a 2025 viral video filmed in Bhutan showed Indian traveller Stephen T criticising fellow Indian tourists for being excessively loud at a serene tourist location.There have been situations where Indian tourists have been recorded singing and dancing at locations including a Sydney train, Switzerland's Mount Titlis and even near a World War II memorial.Here, it’s important to understand that celebrating Indian culture is not the problem.Indian tourists dancing Garba at a cultural festival and singing during a private tour or at an event is very different from turning a crowded bus, airport operational area or solemn memorial into an impromptu dancing or singing stage.Online reactionsOne user wrote, “For those who think it’s cool to sing louder in public transportation in German it’s not allowed to sing louder or bagging or listening louder music it’s written in the buses”“Civic sense died here…”“Why only Gujaratis are happy outside India? 🤣🤣🤣🤣”“Why gujjus why?”“Always Gujarati 👏👏👏”Travel etiquette is part of travelling wellInternational travel is not simply about getting a visa, and ticking destinations off a list.On public transport, that can mean keeping conversations at a reasonable volume, using headphones and allowing other passengers their personal space.None of this requires tourists to abandon their personality. It simply requires awareness of the place and environment.The German bus video may eventually disappear from social media, replaced by the next viral travel controversy. But the conversation it has triggered is worth having.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: A Minnesota woman paid $500 to overnight a box she said held cookbooks; a shipping worker opened it with police and found $30,000 in cash meant for scammers
articles.summary: US News: What looked like an ordinary overnight shipment turned into a scam intervention after a Minnesota shipping company worker became suspicious of a woman.
articles.body: What looked like an ordinary overnight shipment turned into a scam intervention after a Minnesota shipping company worker became suspicious of a woman's unusually urgent request. The woman had arrived at Graphic Mailbox in Northfield, Minnesota, last week hoping to send a package to Texas. She was prepared to pay $500 for overnight delivery and told staff that the box contained cookbooks. But her behaviour raised questions, and an employee's decision to take a closer look ultimately helped prevent her from losing $30,000. According to CBS Minnesota, which reported the incident, the shipping employee involved noticed that the woman appeared frantic and seemed to have rehearsed answers to questions about the package. When the employee's manager and police became involved, the box was opened and its contents revealed a large amount of cash. The woman had been convinced by scammers to send the money to strangers.Suspicious shipping requestThe incident began when the woman walked into Graphic Mailbox in Northfield with a package she wanted to send to Texas. According to CBS Minnesota, Graphic Mailbox employee Alice Castro immediately noticed that something seemed unusual. The woman appeared frantic and gave very specific answers to questions, almost as though she had prepared them in advance. Another detail also stood out. The woman was willing to spend $500 to have the package delivered overnight. She told the staff that the box contained cookbooks. However, the combination of her behaviour, the urgency of the shipment and the large amount she was paying for delivery prompted the employee to become concerned. Rather than simply processing the shipment, Castro and her manager, Terri Sim, became involved.Police uncover cashThe situation took a more serious turn when police were contacted and the package was examined. Inside the box were not cookbooks, but $30,000 in cash. The money was being sent to people the woman did not personally know. She had been instructed to send the cash after scammers convinced her that there was a problem with her financial accounts. Sim told CBS Minnesota that the woman said she had been told her accounts were hacked. The woman also reportedly acknowledged that she had never fallen for this kind of scam before, but said the people contacting her had been convincing. The discovery meant that the package never left the shipping facility.Woman gets money backBecause the shipment was stopped before it reached its destination, the woman was able to recover the money. She also received a refund of the $500 overnight shipping fee she had paid. For Sim, the episode was more than simply stopping a suspicious package. She told CBS Minnesota that after realising what had happened, she walked around the counter, hugged the woman and reassured her that everything would be okay. The incident highlights how scammers can pressure people into making decisions they might otherwise question. Rather than directly asking victims to hand over money in person, criminals may convince them to withdraw large amounts of cash and send it through shipping services.A timely interventionThe incident serves as a reminder that scams can be convincing enough to make otherwise unusual requests seem reasonable. In this case, a simple decision by a shipping employee to ask questions created an opportunity to uncover what was really happening. The intervention also highlights the value of paying attention to warning signs, particularly when a transaction involves unusual urgency or a significant amount of money. By taking the situation seriously rather than treating it as a routine shipment, the employee helped interrupt the scam before it could cause a major financial loss.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
